newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Beef back in France after mad cow crisis.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Beef back in France after mad cow crisis.

text.p: Beef is making a modest comeback in France after the mad cow crisis.

From supermarkets to Parisian bistrots, consumption has picked up after a slump in mid-1996, dispelling pessimism that beef is about to slide off menus for ever in the country that gave the world haute cuisine.

But French consumption of everything from steak tartare to boeuf bourguignon is still well below that before Britain's shock announcement in March 1996 that bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) might be transmitted to people.
And rivals like poultry, fish and pork have snatched markets beef farmers may never recapture.
"There has been a marked recovery in consumption in recent months," said Gerard David of the national meat board OFIVAL.
"Barring bad news, we expect consumption should rise about five percent in 1997 from the depressed levels of 1996. But that would still put it below 1995 levels," he said.

Hoping to consolidate the fragile rebound, the beef industry is mounting a 50 million franc ($8.8 million) advertising campaign on television and in the press, focusing on quality and strict controls on the origin of French meat.
"The good taste of our regions," one advertisment says.
CONSUMPTION DOWN LESS THAN IN MANY EUROPEAN COUNTRIES
OFIVAL estimates that overall beef consumption fell about nine percent in 1996 -- less than in many other European countries -- to 1.45 million tonnes from 1.59 million in 1995 over fears of BSE.

At the height of the crisis in mid-1996, French beef consumption crashed about 20 percent from the previous year amid fears that eating beef could trigger a new variant of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD), which is fatal to humans.
By the end of 1996, consumption had clawed back to around six percent below levels of a year ago. Prices also slumped followed by a slight rebound.

Michel Guegan, a butcher selling everything from wild boar to poultry in Paris' central Rue Montorgueil, said "beef sales have risen a bit recently but many businesses nearly went under because of the British government."
He added ruefully: "It'll be a long time before I take my holidays in Britain."

Among bright spots in France, consumption of some brands of beef -- such as from Charolais or Limousin breeds of cattle which have not been associated with the disease -- is running above levels before the crisis.
Among beef worst hit is unspecified meat, often from old dairy cows. Most of France's 26 cases of mad cow disease have been in dairy herds in Brittany and Normandy in the northwest.
Butcher Guegan said that markets for tripe had all but collapsed and things were not much better for liver and kidneys.
CHIRAC LOYAL TO CALF'S HEAD SPECIALITY

But President Jacques Chirac is sticking to his favourite dish, tete de veau (calf's head stew). Many people have gone off such specialities after a ban on sales of brains, spinal cord and eyes of cows over six months of age for human consumption.
"He still eats it regularly. He hasn't changed his habits," said an official at Chirac's office.
Even before the mad cow crisis, beef consumption had been on a long slow slide in France as health-conscious consumers switched to fish and meats perceived as having less fat.
"It will be hard to raise beef consumption in the long term. But it's feasible to ensure that it doesn't fall any further," said Louis Orenga, director of the industry's meat information centre.

He said that perhaps four percent of French people had stopped eating beef completely. "Others are not yet reassured," he said, adding they were the target of the advertisting that says that France can trace all its animals via identity cards.
FRANCE LED BAN ON BRITISH BEEF IMPORTS

France was the first country to impose a ban on imports of British beef in March 1996, amid fears that now-banned British feed made from ground-up cows had helped spread the disease by turning the herbivores into cannibals.

France has also introduced signs for butchers guaranteeing the origin of meat. Consumers seem not to have been put off by the unfortunate choice of the initials "VF" for these signs, standing for "Viande Francaise" (French Meat) but also for "Vache Folle" -- "Mad Cow" in French.
France has also been helped by having only a tiny number of reported cases of mad cow disease. Its 26 cases compare with some 160,000 in Britain, the country hardest hit.

McDonalds Corp, challenging the traditional bistrot fare with its hamburgers, opened 113 restaurants in France in 1996, raising its the total in France to 541. The firm declined to say whether the crisis has slowed the opening of new outlets.
Even restaurants in Paris with the word "boeuf" (beef) in their names say times are getting less gloomy.
"More people are eating beef again. But the biggest change has been a shift towards fish," said Philippe Dubreuil, chef at the Boeuf sur le Toit restaurant off the Champs Elysees.
The Boeuf Grille restaurant across the city has added poultry and fish to its menu, dominated by steaks.
And the Hard Rock Cafe in Paris, closed for two weeks in November after France concluded it had illegally imported beef from Britain, also says the crisis is fading.

"January and February are never the best months for restaurants, but this year they're no worse than 1996," a spokeswoman said. The American-style restaurant says the disputed beef came legally from Ireland via Britain.
